01 Antidepressants · class card

TCAs

tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) · amitriptyline · clomipramine · desipramine · doxepin · imipramine · nortriptyline · protriptyline

Key point
  • Tricyclics block muscarinic, alpha-1 and histamine H1 receptors besides reuptake dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, confusion; orthostatic hypotension; sedation and weight gain
  • Fatal at relatively low doses: cardiac fast sodium channels blocked wide QRS and ventricular arrhythmia, the usual cause of death
  • Tertiary amines (amitriptyline most) are the most anticholinergic and sedating; tricyclics are relatively contraindicated in older adults, and if one is needed, a secondary amine such as nortriptyline
Drugs

Amitriptyline: tertiary; the most anticholinergic

Clomipramine Anafranil: tertiary; the most serotonergic

Doxepin Silenor (3 or 6 mg, for sleep): tertiary; strong H1 block

Imipramine: tertiary

Nortriptyline Pamelor: secondary; among the least anticholinergic

Desipramine Norpramin: secondary; among the least anticholinergic

Protriptyline: secondary The two amine groupsTertiary amines lean toward serotonin reuptake block and are more anticholinergic and sedating. Secondary amines lean toward norepinephrine reuptake block and are less of both.

Mechanism

Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake blocked effects on mood and pain

Muscarinic block anticholinergic effects; alpha-1 block orthostatic hypotension; H1 block sedation, weight gain

Cardiac fast sodium channels blocked slower conduction QRS widening, ventricular arrhythmia AnalogyAnalogy from the source: the sodium-channel block resembles class IA antiarrhythmics such as quinidine.

Gamma-aminobutyric acid type A (GABA-A) antagonism seizures

Uses

Depression that has not answered first-line drugs

Clomipramine: obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), second line after selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)

Imipramine: enuresis, second line after desmopressin and rarely used

Amitriptyline, nortriptyline at low doses: neuropathic pain, postherpetic neuralgia, migraine prophylaxis Pain and headacheNeuropathic pain: a tricyclic or a gabapentinoid comes first. Migraine prophylaxis: tricyclics are second line. Amitriptyline is the first-line preventive for chronic tension headache. Tricyclics also help diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome and fibromyalgia.

Doxepin: insomnia, from its histamine block Doxepin labelSilenor, low-dose doxepin, is labeled for insomnia with trouble staying asleep.

Adverse effects

Anticholinergic: dry mouth, blurry vision, constipation, urinary retention, fast pulse, confusion; worst with amitriptyline Other effectsTricyclics can also cause gastroparesis; respiratory depression and hyperpyrexia are listed too.

Alpha-1: orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, reflex tachycardia falls in older adults

H1: sedation, more appetite, weight gain; sedation adds to delirium in older adults

Reuptake: sexual dysfunction (low libido, anorgasmia), tremor

GABA-A antagonism: seizures Clomipramine labelOn the Anafranil label, seizure is the most significant risk of the drug.

Cardiac: QRS widening; QT prolongation torsades de pointes

Abrupt stop cholinergic rebound: nausea, vomiting, sweating, headache, muscle aches, irritability, insomnia

Tricyclic overdoseConfusion, seizures, hot dry skin, big pupils, low blood pressure and a wide QRS; can look well at first and then worsen fast

No physostigmine in a tricyclic overdose: it can worsen the cardiotoxicity

If the QRS is over 100 ms, or a ventricular arrhythmia or hypotension appears, choose a sodium bicarbonate infusion.

Serotonin syndromeTypically fever, mental status changes, autonomic instability, hyperreflexia and clonus; often with another serotonergic drug

If serotonin syndrome appears, choose stopping every serotonergic drug.

Interactions, by result
Combined withResultRule
A monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI), or one stopped inside its washout Serotonin syndromeNever together
Fluoxetine, paroxetine, other cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6) blockers; quinidine, cimetidineTricyclic level rises; a stable patient can turn toxicConsider a lower dose
Other anticholinergic drugs, eg, clozapineAnticholinergic toxicity Electrocardiogram (ECG) if toxicity appears
AlcoholStronger effect; more danger in an overdoseWarn the patient
Monitoring and limits
WhenCheckWhy
Before startingPotassium; an ECG at 40 or older, with cardiac symptoms, or on a QT-prolonging drug such as methadoneAn abnormal result adds to the arrhythmia risk
Conduction disease (bundle branch or heart block, long QT); coronary artery diseaseConduction disease: do not use; coronary disease: avoidQT prolongation and arrhythmia
Recovery from a recent myocardial infarctionDo not useThe nortriptyline and amitriptyline labels both warn about the acute recovery period
Epilepsy, angle-closure glaucoma, older agePrescribe cautiously, with close monitoringLower seizure threshold; pupil dilation; anticholinergic effects and falls
Suicide riskA small supply, such as 1 weekFatal at relatively low doses
StoppingTaper over weeks to monthsAvoids cholinergic rebound

Practice
  1. 74-year-old woman started on amitriptyline for postherpetic neuralgia 2 weeks later: new confusion, dry mouth, constipation could not void this morning; bladder felt above the pubis pulse 104/min · pupils large · blood pressure steady on standing → Muscarinic receptor blockade → amitriptyline, the most anticholinergic tricyclic, blocks muscarinic receptors, so the mouth dries, the bowel and bladder stall, the pulse quickens and an older brain clouds; alpha-1 block would drop her pressure on standing, and H1 block would sedate
  2. 38-year-old man took imipramine for 2 years stopped it on his own 3 days ago now nausea, vomiting, sweating, headache, aching muscles, irritability, poor sleep temperature normal · pupils normal · reflexes normal, no clonus · no new drugs → Cholinergic rebound → the long muscarinic block ends at once, so cholinergic activity overshoots: nausea, vomiting, sweating, headache, muscle aches, irritability and insomnia; a slow taper prevents it; no drug was added and he has no clonus or fever
  3. 79-year-old man with painful diabetic neuropathy in both feet a low-dose tricyclic is planned benign prostatic hyperplasia with a slow stream; mild constipation electrocardiogram normal · potassium normal · no conduction disease · no glaucoma → Nortriptyline → nortriptyline and desipramine, the secondary amines, block muscarinic receptors least, so they are the tricyclics for an older adult; amitriptyline blocks them most, and doxepin, also a tertiary amine, is strongly anticholinergic and sedating
